questions.topic: Tissue concept and plant meristematic tissue
questions.question_text: Q: Explain the structure and function of xylem. List its components.
questions.answer: Xylem is a complex permanent tissue that transports water and minerals from roots to leaves in a unidirectional manner. Its components are: (1) Tracheids - elongated dead cells with tapered ends; (2) Vessels - long tubular dead cells; (3) Xylem parenchyma - living cells storing food; (4) Xylem fibres - dead, thick-walled cells providing support.
questions.explanation: See detailed answer above. Key points must be covered for full marks.

questions.topic: Tissue concept and plant meristematic tissue

questions.topic: Tissue concept and plant meristematic tissue
questions.question_text: Q: In a biology lab, students examine a slide showing a tissue with dead cells having extremely thick, pitted walls. The teacher says this tissue makes up a coconut shell. Which tissue is it?
questions.answer: Sclerenchyma tissue. It consists of dead cells with thick, lignified walls that provide mechanical strength, making up structures like coconut shells.
questions.explanation: Sclerenchyma fibres and sclereids form hard protective structures in plants.

questions.question_text: [DIAGRAM QUESTION] Study the diagram of a plant cell showing different tissues. Label the tissue found at the growing tip of the root.
questions.answer: The tissue at the growing tip of the root is meristematic tissue (specifically, root apical meristem). It consists of small, densely cytoplasmic cells with large nuclei that are actively dividing.

questions.topic: Plant permanent tissues - Parenchyma, Collenchyma, Sclerenchyma
questions.question_text: Q: Describe the three types of meristematic tissue with their locations and functions.
questions.answer: Meristematic tissue consists of actively dividing cells. (1) Apical meristem is at root and shoot tips; it causes the plant to grow longer. (2) Lateral meristem (cambium) is in stems and roots; it increases girth (secondary growth). (3) Intercalary meristem is at nodes (e.g., grass); it allows regrowth after grazing or cutting. All three produce new cells that can differentiate into permanent tissue.
questions.explanation: See detailed answer above. Key points must be covered for full marks.

questions.question_text: Q: A student cuts a young plant stem and sees water oozing out from the cut end. Which tissue is releasing this water, and why?
questions.answer: Xylem tissue is releasing water. Xylem vessels are dead, hollow tubes that conduct water. When cut, the water column inside is exposed and oozes out due to root pressure.
questions.explanation: Xylem vessels under root pressure release water when cut - this is called bleeding and is common in many plants.

questions.question_text: Q: During a harvest festival in rural India, farmers store potatoes in cool, dark cellars. Which plant tissue makes this possible, and why?

questions.topic: Animal muscle tissue and nervous tissue
questions.question_text: Q: Explain how connective tissue is different from epithelial tissue in structure.
questions.answer: Epithelial tissue has tightly packed cells arranged in sheets with minimal matrix. It covers surfaces and lines cavities. Connective tissue has cells scattered throughout a large extracellular matrix. Examples: bone, blood, cartilage, tendons. The matrix determines the tissue's properties (solid in bone, fluid in blood).
questions.explanation: See detailed answer above. Key points must be covered for full marks.

questions.explanation: Answer: Hard, thick-walled (dead). Parenchyma has thin walls and is soft (stores food), while sclerenchyma has thick lignified walls and is dead at maturity (provides strength).

questions.topic: Animal muscle tissue and nervous tissue
questions.question_text: Q: A person with a bone fracture is told that their bone is a type of connective tissue. Why is bone classified as connective tissue even though it is hard?
questions.answer: Bone is classified as connective tissue because its cells (osteocytes) are embedded in a hard, mineralised matrix. The matrix is the key feature of connective tissue.
questions.explanation: All connective tissues have cells scattered in an extracellular matrix. In bone, the matrix is hardened with calcium salts.
